venues.d: The best hotel in the world — a vertical estate on the Kowloon waterfront, with the whole harbour at its feet.
A serene, art-filled sanctuary above the city — the quietest luxury in Hong Kong.
The grande dame of Central since 1963 — the address the city measures itself against.
The grand old lady of the Far East — colonnaded, colonial and utterly iconic since 1928.
The surest hands in the city, above the harbour — service you never have to think about.
The world's highest hotel — floors 102 to 118 of the ICC tower, with clouds below the window.
A jewel-box house of just 129 rooms — the most personal of the city's grand hotels, with butler service throughout.
The reborn waterfront legend — floor-to-ceiling harbour glass and the finest island view in the city.

venues.n: Mandarin Oriental The Landmark, Hong Kong
venues.d: A discreet, design-led hideaway above the Landmark's luxury boutiques — pure Central, no harbour, all calm.

venues.n: The Murray, Hong Kong, a Niccolo Hotel
venues.d: A 1960s modernist landmark reborn — soaring arched windows and a garden setting rare in Central.
A grand Art Deco house on the harbour, with one of the city's great outdoor pools and gardens.
Old-world grandeur above Pacific Place — chandeliers, a 16-storey mural, and Petrus high in the sky.
A warm, established harbourside house on the Kowloon side — grand, generous, and reliably excellent.
A high-energy design tower sharing the ICC with the Ritz-Carlton — the rooftop pool is the highest in the city.
A design-forward urban retreat with a vertical garden wall and a genuinely local Hong Kong soul.
A polished, high-floor house above Pacific Place — dependable, central, and quietly grand.
A capable, comfortable Pacific Place tower — big, well-run, and easy for business or family.
A refined European-style house in the heart of Kowloon's shopping and dining quarter.
A serene atrium-garden hotel on the Kowloon side — quietly excellent, and a local secret.
A dependable harbourfront address built into Harbour City — shopping, ferries and the Star Ferry at the door.

venues.n: The Peninsula Hong Kong — Peninsula Suite
venues.d: Two floors, a private terrace and the harbour laid out below — the grandest suite on the Kowloon side.
Richard Ekkebus's dairy-free, produce-led French — newly promoted to three stars after seventeen years.
Umberto Bombana's grand Italian — the only three-star Italian restaurant outside Italy.
French haute cuisine and a legendary cheese trolley, high over the harbour.
Chef Yeung Koon Yat's temple to abalone — the most revered Cantonese kitchen in the city.
An Edomae omakase of the very highest order — the fish flown from Tokyo daily.
Refined, classical Cantonese in a hushed silk-lined room — three stars, decades in the making.
Chef Hideaki Sato's 'travel through life' — French technique, Japanese soul, tiny and exact.
Vicky Cheng's contemporary Chinese — the second-highest a Hong Kong restaurant has ever placed in the world.
Old Hong Kong Cantonese with a conscience — free-range, local, seasonal, and quietly world-beating.
A precise, seasonal Franco-Japanese tasting menu in a serene Central room.
The first Chinese restaurant in the world to hold three stars — now two, still peerless Cantonese.
Classical Cantonese with jade tableware and a full-frontal harbour view.
Delicate, luminous French cooking in a light-filled St. Regis room.
Alvin Leung's 'X-treme Chinese' — provocative, technical, unlike anywhere else.
An intimate, members'-club-feel Italian from the Bombana school — precise and grown-up.
Refined Sichuan and Cantonese in a jewel-box setting — heat handled with real finesse.
Vicky Lau's 'edible poetry' — a French-Chinese ode to Hong Kong, told in delicate courses.
Grand Cantonese on the 102nd floor — the finest dim sum in the sky.
Polished, classical Cantonese from a celebrated master — quietly one of Central's best.
David Lai's market-driven European bistro cooking — no menu, endless charm, always full.
Ricardo Chaneton's Latin-American-accented cooking — the flavours of his roots, refined.
Antimo Merone's ode to Campania — soulful, personal southern-Italian cooking.
Agustin Balbi's Argentine-Spanish-Japanese kitchen — a deeply personal tasting menu.
Vicky Cheng's original — a Chinese-French counter of great craft, above his flagship WING.
David Toutain protégé's plant-forward, nature-led cooking — green, precise and quietly radical.
The Beijing sensation's Hong Kong outpost — pristine Taizhou seafood and yellow croaker.
Milanese cooking done with real heart — nose-to-tail Italian, and a Bib to prove the value.
The first Punjabi restaurant in the world to hold a Michelin star — tandoor-fired and proudly Indian.
Chef Manav Tuli's modern Indian inside the world's best hotel — bright, spiced, beautifully judged.
Julien Royer's French cooking in a restored heritage house — classical, warm, immaculate.
Simon Rogan's farm-to-table ethos, translated to Hong Kong — hyper-seasonal and green.
Grand French dining on the 56th floor — chandeliers, a great wine list, and the harbour beyond.
The most storied French dining room in Asia — grand, gilded, and going strong since 1953.
Anne-Sophie Pic's delicate, aromatic French in a Baccarat-crystal setting overlooking the harbour.
Refined Cantonese on the 25th floor of the grande dame — a jewel-box of a dining room.
Art Deco Cantonese in the Peninsula — dim sum, roast goose and a famous tea menu.
Sumptuous, red-and-gold classical Cantonese — a grand-hotel banquet done properly.
The yakitori izakaya that changed how Hong Kong eats out — every part of the bird, no reservations.
A glamorous temple to the world's finest beef, in a heritage former bank hall.
A neo-Parisian bistro of real soul — the roast chicken has a devoted following.
A one-star roast-goose shop from the Yung Kee dynasty — crisp skin, no ceremony, always a queue.
A tiny, tiled roast-goose canteen with a Michelin star — the roast goose over rice is the reason.
A congee-and-noodle institution since the 1940s — wonton noodles that earned a star.
Modern Cantonese comfort food with swagger — the wagyu short rib and roast goose bring the crowds.
The New York Italian-American theatre — tableside caesar, veal parm, and a room that never quietens.
Honest, generous Sicilian home cooking in a warm neighbourhood room.
The Peninsula's tiny Swiss chalet — fondue and raclette, unchanged and beloved for decades.
A 1930s Cantonese tea house frozen in time — trolley dim sum, teak booths, living history.
Refined Cantonese in a 1930s-Shanghai-tai-pan-mansion setting, overlooking the harbour.
The grande dame's grill — a Terence Conran room, a seafood bar, and old-Hong-Kong glamour.
The 'tycoons' canteen' — old-money Cantonese banqueting, abalone and roast suckling pig.
An art-filled Cantonese salon with a garden terrace — dim sum among rotating exhibitions.
Opulent, classical Cantonese in a grand-hotel room — a benchmark for the old-school banquet.
A long-revered name for abalone, seafood and refined Cantonese classics.
A modern Korean 'hansik' tasting menu of real refinement — the best Korean fine dining in town.

Ride Asia's oldest funicular (1888) up the mountainside, then walk the flat 3.5km Peak Circle Walk for the postcard sweep over the harbour and skyscraper canyon. Come at dusk to catch the towers switch on; a private car and skip-the-line tram booking spares the family the notorious queue.

The green-and-white ferries have crossed the harbour since 1888 and remain the cheapest, most cinematic ride in the city. Sit on the open upper deck between Tsim Sha Tsui and Central at sunset with the whole skyline gliding past on both sides.

Every night at 8pm, around 40 buildings on both sides of the harbour perform a synchronised light-and-laser show. Watch from the Tsim Sha Tsui promenade or, for a private angle, book a junk cruise so the family sees it from the water.

venues.n: Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade & Avenue of Stars
venues.d: A breezy harbour-front walk with the finest head-on view of Hong Kong Island's skyline, past the Bruce Lee statue and handprints of Cantonese cinema legends. Ends near the Clock Tower, a lone relic of the old Kowloon railway terminus.

Herzog & de Meuron's vast museum of 20th- and 21st-century visual culture — design, moving image, architecture and Asian contemporary art — with a giant LED facade facing the harbour. One of the largest museums of modern visual culture in the world; the rooftop and harbour-view galleries reward an unhurried afternoon.

A striking golden building showing treasures on rotating loan from Beijing's Forbidden City — imperial jade, ceramics, paintings and court life — curated for a modern audience. Pairs naturally with M+ next door for a full culture day.

venues.n: Tai Kwun — Centre for Heritage & Arts
venues.d: The beautifully restored former Central Police Station, Magistracy and Victoria Prison, now a compound of galleries, courtyards, boutiques and restaurants. Wander the granite cells and colonial verandahs, then eat well; it is one of the city's most discreet, unhurried spots.

Hong Kong's most atmospheric temple, dedicated to the gods of literature and war, its dim hall hazed with enormous hanging incense coils. A short, calm stop on the way up steep Ladder Street and Hollywood Road's antique galleries.

venues.n: Tian Tan Buddha (Big Buddha) & Po Lin Monastery
venues.d: Climb 268 steps to the world's largest outdoor seated bronze Buddha, serene above the Lantau hills, beside the century-old Po Lin Monastery. The monastery's famous vegetarian canteen is fully veg and Jain-friendly-adjacent — a rare, easy meal for plant-based families.

A 25-minute glass-cabin glide over the sea, the airport and North Lantau's green ridges to Ngong Ping village and the Big Buddha. Splurge on a Crystal Cabin with a glass floor; the panorama is the reason to come even before the Buddha.

venues.a: Shek O / Southern District, Hong Kong Island
venues.d: The city's most loved ridge hike — a gentle, undulating spine with sweeping views over Shek O, Tai Long Wan and the South China Sea, ending at a beach. Around 8km and family-doable; a driver can meet you at the Big Wave Bay end.

Extraordinary hexagonal volcanic rock columns and sea-carved sedimentary formations across the eastern New Territories, best seen by boat from Sai Kung. Charter a private sampan or junk to reach the sea arches and coves in comfort.

venues.n: Sai Kung & the East Country Parks
venues.d: A relaxed fishing town with a live seafood harbour-front, gateway to Hong Kong's cleanest beaches and the MacLehose Trail. Hire a boat to Tai Long Wan's white-sand bays — the closest thing the city has to a private island day.

A vivid, busy Taoist temple where worshippers shake fortune sticks and consult soothsayers, surrounded by a serene Good Wish Garden and koi ponds. Said to 'make every wish come true' — a colourful, welcoming stop for multi-generational visitors.

venues.n: Chi Lin Nunnery & Nan Lian Garden
venues.d: A vast Tang-dynasty-style wooden monastery built without a single nail, beside a meticulously landscaped classical garden with a golden pavilion and lotus ponds. Utterly tranquil, free, and home to a refined vegetarian restaurant behind a waterfall.

Kowloon's classic after-dark bazaar of stalls, fortune-tellers, Cantonese opera singers and open-air dai pai dong seafood. Loud, theatrical and full of old-Hong-Kong character; go early evening with the family before the crowds thicken.

The city's grittiest, most authentic district — fabric and bead streets, electronics arcades, and some of Hong Kong's best cheap eats and third-wave coffee. A design-lover's treasure hunt; go with a guide to find the Michelin-listed street food.

Hong Kong's antiques spine, lined with serious dealers in Ming ceramics, jade and Chinese furniture, plus the flea-market bric-a-brac of Cat Street (Upper Lascar Row). The place for collectors to source with provenance and arrange discreet shipping home.

A former police married-quarters block reborn as a hive of independent Hong Kong designers, jewellers and craft studios. Ideal for finding one-of-a-kind gifts and meeting the makers, with a quiet courtyard cafe to regroup.

Ride the world's longest outdoor covered escalator system uphill through the layered lanes of SoHo and NoHo, hopping off for galleries, wine bars and global restaurants. The easiest way to graze Central's dense dining scene on foot.

Board a double-decker tram — running since 1904 — and ride the whole north shore from Kennedy Town to Shau Kei Wan for the price of a coffee. Grab the front upper-deck seat for a slow, open-window film reel of street life.

A car-free island of green hills, a gentle family walk between Yung Shue Wan and Sok Kwu Wan, and waterfront seafood restaurants at the end. A slow, restorative half-day escape barely 30 minutes by ferry from Central.

A dumbbell-shaped fishing island with a bustling harbour, seafood shacks, a small beach and pirate-cave legends, plus the springtime Bun Festival. Rent bikes and let children roam the car-free lanes; utterly unhurried.

A photogenic stilt-house village on Lantau's west coast, where Tanka fishing families live over the water and shops sell dried seafood and shrimp paste. Take a short boat ride to spot pink dolphins, then stay across the water at the heritage Tai O Heritage Hotel.

Hong Kong's first heritage trail winds through 900 years of Tang-clan history — ancestral halls, a study hall and the territory's only ancient pagoda, the Tsui Sing Lau. A quiet window into pre-colonial walled-village life, far from the tourist crush.

The excellent 'Hong Kong Story' walk-through — from prehistoric coastline to fishing villages, opium wars and the modern metropolis, with life-size street recreations. The single best hour for grounding the family in how this city came to be.

A refreshed, harbour-facing museum of Chinese antiquities, ink painting, and the superb Chih Lo Lou classical Chinese art collection. Calm, air-conditioned galleries with the skyline framed through the windows.

venues.n: Flagstaff House Museum of Tea Ware
venues.d: Hong Kong's oldest surviving colonial building, now a jewel-box museum of Chinese tea culture and Yixing teapots inside leafy Hong Kong Park. Combine with the park's aviary and conservatory for an easy, shaded family morning.

A cliffside marine-and-thrills park spread over a headland, linked by cable car and funicular, with pandas, an enormous aquarium and roller coasters over the sea. A classic full family day for younger children and teens alike.

A compact, well-run Disney park with the world's only Mystic Manor and a growing 'World of Frozen' land. Stay at a park hotel and use a VIP tour host so multi-generational groups skip the queues entirely.

Once a floating fishing community, still crowded with junks and yachts; take a traditional sampan among the boats for a glimpse of old maritime Hong Kong. A short, atmospheric ride that grandparents especially enjoy.

A relaxed seaside town on the island's south coast with a lanes-and-stalls market, breezy waterfront restaurants and the transplanted colonial Murray House. A soft, sunny counterpoint to the city's density.

The island's most fashionable crescent of sand, backed by the wave-shaped Repulse Bay building and the kitsch-but-fun Tin Hau shrine at its eastern end. Genteel, family-safe swimming with beach-club lunching nearby.

A serene Jiangnan-style garden built on the site of the infamous, now-demolished Walled City — the densest place on earth — with a small museum explaining its lawless past. A quiet, curious stop after nearby Kowloon City's Thai and Chiu Chow food.

Climb a hillside path flanked by hundreds of individually posed, life-size golden arhat statues to a hall lined with roughly 13,000 small Buddha figures. Offbeat, uncrowded and genuinely memorable; wear good shoes for the steps.

venues.n: Sik Sik Yuen & the Sha Tin racecourse experience
venues.d: Hong Kong's grand racecourse hosts world-class Wednesday-night and weekend meets in an electric, food-filled atmosphere. Book a members' box or Chinese-cuisine viewing suite for a discreet, catered evening at the heart of the city's oldest passion.

The compact hillside of bars, izakayas and rooftops that empties the offices after dark, ringed by SoHo's more grown-up drinking dens. For a refined evening, aim instead at the harbour-view speakeasies and hotel bars just downhill.
One of the world's highest bars, on the 118th floor of the ICC tower, with the entire harbour and Hong Kong Island laid out below. A memorable sundowner; reserve a window table well ahead.

A 360-degree indoor observation deck on the 100th floor of Hong Kong's tallest building, the best all-weather panorama when the Peak is cloud-covered. Easy and step-free — good for less mobile family members.

Yum cha — the ritual of tea and small plates — is Hong Kong's culinary soul, from trolley-service old-timers to Michelin-starred rooms. Ask an advisor to book a private room and pre-arrange vegetarian and Jain-suitable dishes so nothing is a compromise.

venues.n: Choi Hung Estate & Instagram Hong Kong
venues.d: The rainbow-painted 1960s public-housing estate with its basketball courts has become an icon of graphic Hong Kong. One of a cluster of striking modernist estates (with Montane Mansion's 'Monster Building') that photographers seek out.

A large, well-designed reserve of mangroves, mudflats and boardwalks alive with migratory birds, mudskippers and a resident crocodile. Buggy-friendly and shaded — a genuinely restful nature morning for families with small children.

venues.n: Peak-to-Aberdeen & Pok Fu Lam heritage walk
venues.d: Quiet country trails link the Peak down through Pok Fu Lam past a colonial dairy-farm village and reservoir to the coast. A gentler alternative to Dragon's Back, ending near the seafood of Aberdeen.

Charter a red-sailed junk or a private motor yacht to drift through the harbour at golden hour, drinks in hand, the skyline turning on around you. The city's signature private experience — book the whole boat for the family.

An hour by fast ferry to a Portuguese-Chinese old town of pastel churches, the Ruins of St Paul's, cobbled Senado Square and A-Ma Temple — plus egg tarts and world-class casino resorts. Skip the gaming floors for a private heritage-and-dining day, or the reverse.
Lorenzo Antinori's 'popular Roman bar' — unfussy Italian aperitivi, done so well it became the finest bar on earth.
Jay Khan's temple to agave — 200-plus tequilas and mezcals, and hospitality that redefined the Asian bar.
The Four Seasons' flagship bar — a sustainability-led cocktail programme and rare spirits, poured with hotel-grade polish.
The world's first closed-loop sustainable bar — house ferments, zero waste, and a serious cocktail behind the ethic.
A Hemingway-inspired snug of literary cocktails — once the best bar in Asia, and still a rite of passage.
Antonio Lai's laboratory — the birthplace of molecular mixology in Hong Kong, all foams, mists and multisensory theatre.
A velvet-and-Murano jazz parlour of dark spirits, cigars and live music — the most glamorous late night on the Kowloon side.
The world's highest bar, on the 118th floor of the ICC — cocktails in the clouds, with the whole harbour far below.
A double-height glass room and terrace on the 30th floor of One Peking — the classic full-frontal skyline view with a drink in hand.
A theatrical Japanese-inspired izakaya-bar in the grande dame — jewel-box interiors and one of the city's best cocktail lists.
A tiny bar built entirely on savoury, umami-driven cocktails — the most inventive drinking in the city right now.
Bonnae Gokson's rooftop terrace atop Prince's Building — wrapped around the towers of Central, glamorous and enduring.
A polished terrace bar above Stanley Street with a classic-cocktail pedigree — old-Hong-Kong elegance, done properly.
A drink at the grande dame of Kowloon — the Lobby by day, Philippe Starck's 28th-floor Felix by night, harbour spread below.
The city's original nightlife quarter — a hillside of bars and clubs that spills into the street. Loud, packed, unmissable once.
